interactions.hypothesis: First-half totals depend on first-half pace, which differs from game pace and is team-specific.
A starter's early fouls create the biggest first-half-specific variance.

First-half scoring equals first-half possessions times first-half points per possession; a team that starts fast (high half pace ratio) and shoots above shot quality early gets the product of both advantages, while the second half is not affected, so the effect lives only in the half contract.

A star starter's early foul trouble costs minutes only if the coach sits at two fouls, and costs more if the replacement is a much weaker unit; the net first-half impact is the product of foul probability, benching policy and the gap between starter and substitute.

Once a team reaches the seventh foul in the half its opponent gets one-and-one chances and at the tenth two shots, so the value of each additional foul steps up; teams with 75 percent or better free-throw shooters gain much more than poor ones, producing a threshold-by-skill interaction late in the half.

For 2H contracts that include overtime, the second-half margin distribution is a mixture of the regulation second half and the overtime period, and the probability of reaching overtime depends on the halftime margin and the pregame expectation together; a halftime lead of 15 nearly removes the OT component.

Because the first half has about 33 possessions, a hot or cold shooting start is a larger share of the half outcome for slow teams that have fewer possessions, so the regression weight on recent shooting luck should rise as the expected half possession count falls.

interactions.hypothesis: Title odds are convex in rating and sensitive to single-game variance; high-variance teams are mispriced when ratings alone are used.

Title probability is a product over six games of win probabilities that are probit in rating gap over game sd, so the log-title probability is approximately linear in rating gap and its sensitivity to game sd is largest for the favourite: a modest increase in game variance transfers a large share of title equity from the best team to the field.

Title and qualification probabilities for a bubble or low-seed team depend on the field size and play-in structure: in an expanded field an extra play-in win may be required for the lowest seeds, and the allocation of bids changes who is in at all, so the simulator output is conditional on the format.

The loss of one top player cuts strength by an amount that depends on the replacement and the team's depth; combined with the number of rounds (each with an independent miss probability) the strength distribution of a title contender is a mixture whose lower component holds nontrivial weight, and the favourite's title probability is the weighted sum over states.

A top seed with a double bye plays one fewer game and has an extra rest day, while a lower seed must win four games in four days; the advantage of a bye grows with the length of the bracket and with how thin the team's rotation is, so the fatigue effect depends on the format.

Because title probability is convex in strength, adding uncertainty about March strength raises the title probability of mid-tier contenders and lowers the favourite's (Jensen's inequality on the exponential-like tail), so the same current rating gap yields different odds in November and in February.

The men's and women's tournaments share no games or players, so the combo probability is the product of the two title probabilities; the product makes a combo of two favourites far less likely than either leg, and any shared shock (a school-wide event) would be a small positive correlation only.

In a November event most of a team's rating is still preseason prior, so the event's format matters more when that prior is uncertain: pool play seeded by point differential amplifies rating error into seeding error, while a straight bracket only compounds per-game error.

interactions.hypothesis: Equal-rated teams differ in title odds by remaining schedule and tiebreaker exposure.

The value of a double bye depends on how much better the bye team is than the field: for a dominant team the bye removes two games it would usually win and adds little, while for a top seed only slightly better than seeds 3 to 6 the bye removes two coin-flip-adjacent games and can raise title probability by a third.

Probability of a top-4 finish depends on the distribution of the fourth-best win total in the whole league, which changes with how many strong teams there are; the same team has a lower probability in a league with six contenders than in one with four, and the tie-inclusive rule raises it most when the cutoff is crowded.

The expected share depends on the joint distribution of the top contenders' records, not on each marginal: two equal contenders who rarely lose outside their head-to-head games tie often, halving each share, whereas the same marginals with independent loss patterns produce more sole titles.

Effort changes appear only after a team's stakes cross a threshold: a team that clinched the top seed loses incentive and may rest starters in the final games, while a team one win away from a double bye does not; the effect is a function of leverage computed from the standings simulation.

Seeding ties matter only when they straddle a bye line or a bracket-side boundary; within a seed band they change nothing, but a two-way tie for the last double bye moves one team's path from three wins to four, a discrete jump in championship-game probability.

interactions.hypothesis: Seed outcomes near boundaries depend on late quality wins and committee preferences; model the committee's ranking rather than ratings alone.
Bid-thief probability reduces at-large slots; bubble odds depend jointly on conference tournaments and resume.
Advancement probabilities mix rating-implied and seed-implied base rates; weight by sample size.
Conference strength offsets are uncertain and propagate into SOS and bubble odds.

For teams contending for a one or two seed, predictive ratings and quality wins dominate the committee's ordering, whereas on the bubble the quadrant record and bad losses dominate; the coefficient on predictive ratings relative to resume metrics therefore changes across seed bands.

The number of bid thieves depends on the joint outcomes of 30 conference tournaments, so the distribution of at-large slots available to the bubble is a function of the sum of Bernoulli events with unequal probabilities; a single multi-bid league tournament upset can create a thief at once and change the cutoff for all bubble teams.

If the committee weights recent results more, the same cumulative metrics yield different seeds for teams that peaked early versus those that finished strong; the seed distribution is therefore conditional on trajectory in the last month.

A bubble team's field probability is near zero or one unless its resume sits within a narrow band around the cutoff; games matter a lot only when the resume is in that band, so the leverage of a game is large near the cutoff and small for locks and for teams far outside.

The seed shift for a missing star depends on how much of the team's rating the player carries; for a team whose value is spread across a deep roster the committee has little reason to move it, while for a one-star team the shift may be larger and uncertain in sign.

Upset counts across games in a round are positively correlated through the year's seed-line strength gaps (a weak crop of #2 seeds raises all four 2-15 upset chances together) and negatively linked across rounds (an early upset leaves a weaker team to be upset later or removes an upset chance), so counts are overdispersed relative to independent seed base rates.

An unbeaten season or a 30-win total needs nearly every game won, so its probability averages a steep product of win probabilities over the strength draw; widening strength uncertainty raises these tail probabilities for top teams above the value at the mean rating.

For two named teams to both reach the Round of 16, the seed draw and region placement matter jointly: both being top-4 seeds in different regions makes the joint near the product of marginals, while same-region placement or a possible second-round meeting cuts it sharply.

The same rating gap converts into a larger expected margin in a high-possession game and a smaller one in a low-possession game, so the spread is gap times possession ratio, and the underdog's cover chance is higher in slow games where margin sd is also smaller relative to the number.

Once the expected margin passes roughly 15 to 20 points the game flips into a blowout regime whose end-of-game compression depends on the coach: a lead-protecting coach turns a model margin of 25 into a 14 point cover miss, while a starter-heavy coach does not. Below the threshold the coach term is irrelevant.

Early in the season (before about 8 games) the prior carries the weight and uncertainty is highest, so the weight on the in-season improvement slope should be near zero; by February the same slope is a useful signal. The correct blend depends on games played and on roster continuity.

A starter's absence costs more points for a team with a short rotation and a low-quality replacement than for a deep team; the effect is also larger when the missing player controls the ball, since the replacement changes turnovers and pace as well as scoring.

Home advantage is a three-regime piecewise term: full home court, neutral floor, and semi-home (conference tournaments held in a nearby arena); the team-specific deviation applies to the full-home regime and shrinks toward zero otherwise.

interactions.hypothesis: Strong-defense, slow teams cut totals non-additively because tempo control and half-court defense compound.
Offenses boosted by recent hot three-point shooting are overrated for totals; regress by 3PA share.
Whistle-heavy games lengthen games and add FT points when teams are good FT shooters.
A missing primary ball handler slows tempo and lowers transition scoring, interacting with the efficiency loss.
Close-game late fouling raises totals; the effect is concentrated in games with small spreads.

A strong half-court defence that forces long possessions lowers both the number of possessions and points per possession, so the effect on the total is the product of the two reductions, larger than the sum of separate tempo and defence effects, in slow-tempo teams in particular.

Recent shooting above expectation is regressed toward shot-quality expectation with weight depending on the attempt share: a team with 45 percent of shots from three has far more luck-driven variance, so its recent over-performance should be discounted harder than a rim-based team's.

Extra fouls add points only through free-throw conversion, so the whistle effect on the total is foul count times combined free-throw percentage; a whistle-heavy crew with two poor free-throw teams adds much less than the same crew with two 78 percent teams.

Intentional fouling adds points only if the game is within roughly 8 points with under two minutes left, so the add-on is a step function of projected closeness; in games decided earlier it contributes nothing and the bench-clearing effect pushes the total down. Closeness is the model's competitive-regime probability, not a market spread.

The pace effect of an injury exists only if the missing player is one of the team's primary ball handlers, and its sign differs from a rim-protector absence, so the injury input must be mapped to a role before it can shift the total.

Sharp totals are good, so edges come from availability mixtures, shooting-luck regression and rung-level mispricing.

interactions.hypothesis: Absence of the primary scorer raises usage but lowers efficiency; effect depends on whether the replacement is a same-role scorer.
Zone defense lowers drive-based scoring and raises three-point attempts, changing scoring distribution by role.
High rungs are sensitive to the probability of a lopsided game; mixture model is required.
Fast tempo increases attempts but late fouls matter more in tight games for FT points.

When a primary scorer is out, a remaining scorer's usage rises but his efficiency falls because the extra shots are lower quality and defences key on him; the net points gain flattens (or even reverses) as usage climbs beyond about 28 percent, particularly if the replacement is not a same-role scorer.

For a starter on a favourite, the chance of crossing a high points rung is dominated by the probability of staying in a competitive game; in the blowout regime minutes drop by about 8 and points by about 6, so the high rung is a mixture and lower rungs are relatively insensitive.

Attempts equal usage share times team possessions, so a high-usage player in a fast game has a multiplicative boost to volume and variance, in a way that an additive tempo term cannot capture for large usage.

Late free throws accrue only if the game stays within about six points inside the last two minutes and only to the ball handlers on the floor, so the contribution is a step function of closeness times role, nearly zero for bigs and for blowouts.

The weight on observed shooting streaks relative to the shot-location expectation should fall as the number of attempts grows and rise when the player's shot mix changed (new role or new team), so the regression target is conditional on sample size and on role change.

Attempts depend on usage and role (stable but changing with teammates), efficiency on shot quality, opponent defense style and shooting regression; minutes on foul trouble and blowouts. Teammate absences concentrate shots on remaining scorers in short rotations; tempo scales attempts.

In competitive games a team's points rise roughly half-for-half with the margin, but once the expected margin passes about 15 the favourite's points stop rising (starters sit, possessions shorten) while the underdog's points are propped up by late fouls, so the slope flips between regimes.

When a slow-tempo team meets a fast team, whose pace wins depends on each team's elasticity: scoring volume equals the elasticity-weighted tempo times points per possession, so a team that dictates pace adds or removes points for the opponent too.

The favourite's total beyond the starters' minutes is the product of the probability of a blowout and the bench unit's scoring rate in that scenario; both are uncertain and positively linked to coach style, so they should be modelled jointly instead of averaged.

A team's free-throw points are its drawing rate times the opponent's foul propensity times conversion; a rim-attacking team against a foul-prone defence has a larger amplification than either factor suggests alone, in close games late in the half when the bonus applies.

Because the contract pays only the single highest score, a team's chance rises convexly with its expected possessions relative to the other teams in the round: a few extra possessions move a fast team from near the top to the top far more often than they lift a slow team, and the effect grows with the number of games in the round.

cbb.ap_voter_ballot_panel.measurement: Collect each weekly ballot (voter id, ranks 1 to 25); for each voter-team-week compute rank change as a function of the team's result (win/loss, opponent rank, margin, site), prior rank and a voter fixed effect; fit a mixed model with voter random slopes using 5 seasons; simulate the poll as the sum of voter points from the fitted update rules (25 points for 1st down to 1 for 25th); as-of: previous poll plus results.
cbb.ap_voter_ballot_panel.mechanism: The AP poll aggregates individual ballots published by voter; each voter's update after results has its own inertia and preferences, so the aggregate response to a loss is the sum of heterogeneous responses.
cbb.ap_voter_ballot_panel.rationale: A voter-level model captures both the average reaction to a loss and the dispersion that makes top-two ties or leapfrogs likely; aggregate-only models cannot tell whether a swing is a few extreme voters or broad movement.

inputs.why: Search stage and decision-makers bound timing and how open the candidate set still is.
Calibrated insider reports are the main information arriving during a search.
Programme-building record is how committees rank candidates.
Mass on unlisted candidates and on no permanent hire caps listed probabilities.
Alumni, former-staff and AD links are a strong prior on who is chosen.
Salary, buyout capacity and roster budget decide which candidates are reachable.
Candidate's own season or buyout dates can remove him from a fast search.
Show-cause orders and investigations remove otherwise strong candidates.
General coaching news feed captures vacancy openings and announcements with timestamps.
Point-in-time team ratings are the raw basis for a candidate's measured programme improvement.
Defines permanent versus interim, the Sep 1, 2027 cutoff and No-for-all handling.
Interim coach's results versus a fundamentals-only expectation drive the interim-to-permanent route for this vacancy.
Fundamentals-only pregame expected margins and ratings score the interim's season against expectation without any betting line.
Simulated conference finish, NCAA bid and advancement for the interim's team, and elimination dates of candidates' teams.
Preseason expectation baseline for the interim's team, needed to tell over-performance from inherited talent.
Incumbent departure hazard and succession arrangements set the no-vacancy and coach-in-waiting mass for series opened before a vacancy.

interactions.hypothesis: A finalist or offer report late in a search converts to a hire far more often than the same report in the first days after the opening.
Strong-record sitting coaches are reachable only when offer capacity covers salary plus buyout; below that ratio track record stops mattering.
A candidate still coaching in March loses probability as the transfer-portal window approaches if the school's search is already advanced.
A deferred search lets the interim's season results move his hire probability; with an immediate search they do not matter.

The same report stage converts at different rates depending on search progress: a 'finalist' report two days after a firing is often agent leverage, while one after interviews have closed with a board meeting scheduled is close to decisive.

Track record raises hire probability only once the school's offer capacity exceeds the candidate's salary plus buyout; below that ratio the strongest records are effectively unattainable and mass moves to assistants.

Searches either wait for a preferred candidate still coaching in March or close before the transfer portal opens; which regime applies depends on search age and the school's urgency, flipping the candidate's probability.

Ties scale the odds of a hire roughly proportionally at any track-record level; an alumnus with a modest record can outrank a stranger with a better one, and an AD's prior hire carries the largest multiplier.
Each additional credible report about listed names shrinks the unlisted mass, but the reduction slows as only late surprise hires remain; early surprises are common, late ones rare.

With a deferred search the interim's results matter only while the search is not yet open: a strong season can cancel or shorten the search (regime A), a weak one hands the decision to a conventional search after the season (regime B), so the interim's hire probability switches level at the search start rather than varying smoothly.

The no-hire mass and the unlisted mass are not separable: a retirement with a pre-arranged successor removes both, while a firing opens a conventional search with a large unlisted mass, so the residual masses must be mixed over departure types rather than estimated from all vacancies pooled.

coaching_and_governance_events.label: CBB next permanent head coach (Men's College Basketball Next Coach)
coaching_and_governance_events.mechanism: The outcome is an institutional choice: a vacancy opens, an athletic director (with president, board and often a search firm) builds a candidate list from sitting head coaches, assistants and former players, ranks them on track record, ties and fit, and must win a two-sided negotiation constrained by salary, buyouts, roster budget and each candidate's own season calendar. Reports leak along the way. Settlement counts only a permanent (non-interim) hire before the deadline, so unlisted candidates and interim-only outcomes carry probability mass that all listed markets lose. The blueprint season_outcome is kept only because the catalog schema requires an existing blueprint; this archetype takes none of that blueprint's bracket or committee inputs except through the explicitly listed ones (ratings and bracket simulation are used only to score an interim coach's season and a candidate's elimination date).

Fundamentals-only ensemble supplies win probabilities and margins for the remaining games without betting lines.
Byes, bracket size and neutral sites fix how many games each team plays before the snapshot.
Blowout versus competitive regimes determine how margins translate into the efficiency the algorithm sees.
Late-season absences change expected efficiency in the final games before the snapshot.
Posterior sd of each team's rating and the residual preseason-prior weight set how far a rank can move from November to March.
Versioned wording fixes the ratings page, timestamp and what Yes means.
Settled value and time show which page state the exchange actually read.
Season-horizon variance of AdjEM from the pricing date to Mar 15, combining prior phase-out and true-strength drift; dominant from November to January.
KenPom starts from a preseason prior that is phased out over the season, so the prior's error is a main source of early rank movement.
Returning minutes and transfer integration predict how far a team's true strength departs from its preseason rating as the season develops.
Player impact values convert portal arrivals, freshmen and injuries into expected efficiency changes over the remaining season.
Remaining schedule strength and venue mix set expected margins and how much opponent re-adjustment the team will see before Mar 15.
Conference seeding and tiebreakers decide byes and so the number of conference-tournament games before the snapshot.
Availability-adjusted strength for the active set gives expected game efficiency when a key player is out before the snapshot.
Own and opponent three-point luck in realised efficiency tends to regress, giving an expected direction of AdjEM drift.
Home, away and neutral coding sets the venue adjustment of each game margin entering the rating.
Conference tournaments and early-season events are at neutral or semi-home sites, which changes the venue term of those games.

interactions.hypothesis: A flip needs the per-game update to be large relative to the AdjEM gap, so the same remaining schedule is safe for a team with a wide gap and live for a bunched one.

Extra tournament games add variance to a high-rated team's rank because the rating only falls if it under-performs its expected margin, and bye teams carry less variance than teams that must play three games.
Blowout margins earn diminishing rating credit, so heavy favourites gain little from beating weak conference-tournament opponents while narrow wins can still cost rating.
Rank volatility from November to January is largest for high-churn rosters, because the phased-out prior was least informative for them and true strength moves most.

A rank flips only when the cumulative AdjEM move of the team and its neighbours exceeds the local gap. The probability behaves like a normal-tail crossing in the ratio of gap to per-game update sd times root games left, so risk is low until the ratio falls below about 1.

A first-round bye removes one or two games, so a bye team's rank variance is smaller; a top seed that is knocked out early loses little rating if it still performed close to expectation, whereas deep runs add variance in both directions.

Because large margins are discounted by the algorithm, a high-offence team that wins by 30 gains much less than 3 times the credit of a 10-point win, so projected AdjEM gains from soft opponents are muted and a close win can reduce AdjEM.

A key player's absence lowers true strength immediately, but the rating reflects it only after games are played without him, so a team's rank on Mar 15 can lag its true strength; the lag matters in bunched regions.

Only teams that played a Selection Sunday final can be affected by a delayed overnight refresh or downtime, and only if they sit within a few tenths of a cutoff; the two conditions must hold together, so the risk is a small joint tail.

The variance of AdjEM to Mar 15 depends on the residual weight of the prior: in November a high-churn team's rating can move several points and flip a top-25 position, while by February the same roster churn adds little because results dominate.

kenpom_rating_snapshot.label: KenPom rating rank snapshot
kenpom_rating_snapshot.mechanism: The outcome is the position of a team in a deterministic efficiency-margin list recomputed from all D1 results, read at Mar 15, 2027 12:00pm EST (the Monday after Selection Sunday, with no D1 games scheduled that day). From a November pricing date the horizon is the whole season: the preseason prior is phased out, true strength drifts with roster integration and injuries, and some 28-34 games each move AdjEM by an opponent-adjusted surprise. By March only 0-4 games remain. The probability is an order-statistic crossing problem set by AdjEM gaps, remaining rating variance, update sensitivity and which results the Monday-noon page has processed.
kenpom_rating_snapshot.target: Team's rank on the KenPom ratings at a fixed timestamp (exact rank or top-N)

inputs.why: Chains the regulation tie with per-period repeat-tie rates for 2+ and 3+ overtime rungs.
Fundamentals-only strength gap sets the expected margin around which tie mass is evaluated.
Expected possessions scale the margin sd; fewer possessions raise the probability of a tie.
Three-point volume makes scoring lumpier and widens the margin distribution, lowering tie mass.
Early-season rating uncertainty flattens the expected-margin distribution and raises tie probability for mismatches.
Play-for-tie versus play-for-win policy shifts tie mass only in close finishes; pooled by tier, with coach deviations only when well supported.
Foul carryover reshapes scoring in each OT period and makes repeat-tie rates period-dependent.
Intentional fouling by the trailing team changes the late margin path and the chance it ends level.
Absences move the expected margin, the only strength input to tie probability.
Home advantage shifts the expected margin away from or toward zero.
Rungs count periods played; postponement and cancellation handling are in the text.
Live score, clock, period and foul state dominate the rung probabilities once a game is tied late or in overtime, if priced in play.
Team and closing-lineup FT% plus free-throw rate decide whether intentional-foul sequences end level and drive bonus-heavy OT scoring.

interactions.hypothesis: Tie probability falls steeply in the expected margin, so uncertainty about the margin raises it for mismatches but barely changes it for even games.
Slow, low-three teams have the narrowest margin distributions and the highest tie mass; the two effects compound.
Repeat-tie rates rise or fall across OT periods with foul depletion, so a constant repeat factor misprices the 3+ rung.

Tie probability is a peaked function of the expected margin; averaging it over an uncertain margin raises it for large expected margins (Jensen on the convex tail) and slightly lowers it near zero, so November mismatches carry more OT risk than plug-in estimates suggest.

Margin sd grows with both possessions and three-point share; tie probability scales roughly with the inverse of sd near even games, so slow, low-three matchups compound into the highest regulation tie rates.

End-game policy only matters in games within one or two possessions in the last minute; a play-for-tie coach increases tie mass only in that regime, so its effect scales with the close-game probability.
Once both teams are in the double bonus with starters fouled out, overtime scoring shifts to free throws and the repeat-tie rate changes; the 3+ rung lives almost entirely in this regime.
If the leading team's best free-throw shooters are absent, the fouling strategy of the trailing team becomes more effective, increasing comebacks to a tie in the final minute.

Intentional fouling by the trailing team pays off in proportion to how often it forces free throws times how poorly the leader's shooters convert; a low-FT% closing lineup facing a foul-heavy trailing coach raises both comeback ties and repeat ties in bonus-heavy OTs.

overtime_periods.label: CBB overtime periods played
overtime_periods.mechanism: Reaching N overtime periods requires a tied score at the end of regulation and then N-1 further ties after each five-minute period. The first tie depends on the integer pmf of the regulation margin at zero, set by the strength gap, possessions, three-point lumpiness and end-game decisions; each repeat tie depends on the short-period scoring distribution, which bonus free throws and fouled-out players from foul carryover reshape. Rungs are nested and fall geometrically.
overtime_periods.target: Number of overtime periods played in a game (at least N OT periods)

The drop in poll rank after a loss depends on who the opponent was and where the game was played: a road loss to a top-15 team moves a #1 team down a few places, while a home loss to an unranked team can drop it five or more; the same rating gap implies different poll movement depending on opponent rank and site.

The distinct-#1 count is far into the tail for strikes like 9, where the probability depends strongly and convexly on the per-week change probability: a rise in weekly change probability from 15 to 20 percent multiplies the probability of 9 or more holders several times because it requires many successive changes with new successors.

The probability a named player wins Tournament MOP is the product of his team's probability of winning the title and his share of the vote within a champion; because the first factor is small for most teams (a fraction of a percent) and the second is concentrated in the top player, the product is extremely skewed toward stars on top seeds.

A Final-poll top-10 or exact-rank outcome is decided mostly by the round a team reaches: within a round, pre-tournament AP rank orders teams, but a Final Four run lifts a team past almost any higher-ranked early loser, so the effect of pre-tournament rank on the final rank is large for early exits and small for deep runs.

Each remaining poll is another chance for a never-before #1 team to take the top spot, but late in the season the pool of plausible new holders shrinks to teams already near the top, many of which have held #1 already, so additional polls add progressively fewer new distinct holders to the KXNCAAMBAPCHURN count.

The same 28-win season makes a strong coach-of-the-year case for a team picked to finish mid-conference but almost none for a preseason top-5 team, so the effect of team success on award probability is conditional on (and decreasing in) preseason expectation.

polls_and_awards.label: College basketball polls, #1 rank and awards
polls_and_awards.mechanism: Poll position follows results, opponent rank and voter inertia; the number of distinct #1 teams is driven by upset probability among the top teams and voter reactions to losses. Player awards follow production, team success and narrative. Markets here are driven by schedule structure and voter behaviour, not game-level models alone.
polls_and_awards.target: Which teams hold a poll rank or how many distinct teams hold #1, or an individual award winner.

inputs.why: Team opening-segment scoring profile and opening-possession edge, the closest direct predictor of a first-passage race.
First-passage simulation on alternating possessions with tip-win edge, specific to a first-to-N contract.
Scales the edge by N because races to 10, 25 and 50 weigh luck and rating differently.
Opponent-adjusted offence sets points per possession for the team's unit in the race.
Opponent-adjusted defence sets the points per possession the rival unit concedes in the race.
Opening five and their health decide who is on the floor in the race segment before substitutions.
Late scratches change the starting lineup and thus scoring rate in the opening minutes.
Starter-unit on-floor efficiency is the actual scoring rate in the race window.
Possessions per minute fix how fast the points accumulate and how many tries each side gets.
Early-game pace relative to full game captures slow starts or quick openings by team.
Early three-point reliance drives a scoring distribution with lumpy 3-point jumps and fat tails.
Home court shapes opening-segment scoring through crowd and shooting familiarity.
Bonus and foul counts matter for the race to 50 where free throws may arrive before halftime.
Play-by-play ordering errors can flip close races and settlement lag affects resolution.
Wording defines the first to score N, game original date and postponement window.
Postponement and 48-hour rule decide whether a market resolves or goes to fair price.
Early-season efficiencies are mostly preseason prior, so the uncertainty of the rating gap dilutes its weight in the 25 and 50 races.
Markets list from early November, when the opening-unit scoring rate must be read off the preseason prior and roster churn.
A race to 50 runs to about minute 27 and uses bench units, whose scoring rate differs from the starters'.
If the market trades after tip, the current score gap to N, possession and clock replace pregame inputs as the main predictor.

interactions.hypothesis: The opening-possession tie-break matters most when both starting units score at similar rates, and it fades when one unit's points per possession clearly exceeds the other's.
A starting-lineup change inside the race window moves the unit's scoring rate more than the season rating suggests, so lineup news interacts with unit efficiency.
The same offensive gap converts into a larger race advantage at N=50 than at N=10 because the signal accumulates linearly while noise grows with the square root of possessions.
Bench-unit scoring matters only for races long enough to outlast the starters' first stint, so its weight is near zero at N=10 and material at N=50.

With near-equal points per possession the team with the first possession wins ties in possession count and gains a few percentage points; when one unit's rate is clearly higher the tie-break matters less, so the opening-possession effect depends on the rate gap.

If a regular starter is out, the opening unit is a different five with a different scoring rate and the effect is concentrated in the first segment before the usual rotation resumes; the season's team rating understates this for races to 10.

Signal grows with the number of possessions and noise with its square root, so the effect of the offensive rating gap on the race win probability scales with N; at 10 it is slight, at 50 close to the full-game effect.

Three-point heavy teams produce lumpier scores, and in a fast game more of those attempts occur in the window, increasing the chance of an early 9-0 run and spreading the first-passage time distribution.

Reaching 50 depends on whether bonus free throws begin before the team gets there; once a team enters the bonus the points per possession rises, which switches the late race regime for teams that foul early.

The rating gap should drive N=50 races more than N=10, but in November the gap is mostly prior and uncertain, so the slope on the gap at N=50 should be flatter early in the season and steepen after conference play begins.
Bench units enter after the first media timeouts, so their scoring rate affects only races still open at that point; a weak bench costs a team the race to 50 but not the race to 10.

race_to_n_points.label: CBB race to N points
race_to_n_points.mechanism: Each team's points arrive in discrete possession-by-possession chunks, so the race is a first-passage problem on two alternating scoring processes. The edge comes from the opening five's points per possession (prior-heavy and uncertain early in the season), the jump-ball winner's tie-break, early turnovers and rebounds, the bench units for N=50, and N itself: races to 10 are mostly variance, races to 50 approach the share of points over about 26 minutes. If markets trade in-play, the live score gap to N and possession dominate.
race_to_n_points.target: Which team first reaches N points in a game (first-passage event)

contract_types: Men's College Basketball Conference Stat Leader

inputs.why: Leaderboard max-of-noisy-averages simulation including postseason games and thresholds, the direct model of this contract.
NCAA minimums decide who is eligible, so a leader near the cutoff can be removed from the contest.
Remaining-swing bound shows how locked the leaderboard is given games played and remaining.
Usage and shot share drive points, threes and rebounds per game and persist across games.
Projected minutes scale every counting stat and respond to blowouts, fouls and role.
Injury, suspension and coach decisions reduce games played and can disqualify a candidate.
Postseason and late-season availability risk for the top candidates affects both games and qualification.
Threes made per game is minutes times attempts times a Beta-uncertain make rate, the compound behind the 3PM leader markets.
Three-point attempt volume decides who can lead the made-threes category more than shooting percentage.
Rebounds per game depend on the pool of missed shots and offensive-rebound structure of the team.
Assists per game depend on the potential assists and teammates' make rate, not only the passer.
Transfers and freshmen have no college role history, so the leader pool needs cold-start priors.
Teammate injuries redistribute usage and minutes and can raise a candidate's average.
Per-game sd by role sets how quickly the average converges and how much noise remains.
Counts of games, sites and which are official define the sample size over which the average is built.
Possessions scale the opportunities for counting stats and differ by team across the pool.
Stat provider reliability and correction lag matter for the final official table.
Wording fixes which games count and the minimum thresholds and the non-qualification clause.
Final leader and timing of settlement from past seasons show the lag and source used.
Postseason games count, so each candidate team's expected postseason games set both the qualification denominator and the games still to average.
Settlement source is unseen; conference-office and NCAA tables can differ in minimums, games included and corrections, deciding close races.
Simulated conference tournaments and the NCAA field give the probability of each extra postseason game for a candidate's team.
Conference seeding and byes set the number of conference-tournament games each candidate can add.
Stars on heavy favourites lose minutes in blowouts all season, a systematic drag on their per-game average.
Remaining opponent strength, including soft nonconference slates, shifts per-game production systematically for a candidate.

interactions.hypothesis: Minutes and usage multiply, so a modest rise in either lifts the average more than additively, and role changes after teammate departures or injuries move leaders.
Missed games matter as a cliff once a candidate nears the NCAA minimum, so injury risk is far more costly for a leader close to the threshold.
The same gap between candidates is worth more probability late than early because each remaining game moves an average by less, so race uncertainty collapses as games are played.
A deeper team run raises the team-games denominator, so a candidate who has missed games can fall below the minimum by his team winning.

Points per game equal minutes times usage-driven per-minute scoring, so a 10 percent rise in each gives about 21 percent more, and teammate departures or injuries can raise both together for a candidate.

Eligibility requires a minimum share of games, so a candidate with margin of two games above the threshold who misses three loses all probability; the cost of absence is zero until the threshold and then total.

Early in the season an average moves by up to a point per game and leaders change often; after 25 games it moves by less than a few tenths, so the probability a leader holds rises sharply in the second half of the season.

Made threes are attempts times a noisy make rate; volume gives a stable base and the make rate adds luck, so the 3PM leader is typically a high-volume shooter whose make rate is not extreme and uncertainty is dominated by the rate for low-volume candidates.

A leader on a deep-run team gains postseason games that reduce noise but raise injury exposure, and a leader on an early-eliminated team stops accumulating games, so the effect of tournament depth depends on both the quality of opposition and risk of absence.

Postseason games raise the team-games denominator, so a candidate who has already missed games can lose qualification because his team keeps winning, while extra games also dilute a hot start; the effect exists only for candidates near the minimum.

Expected minutes are scaled down by the share of games that become blowouts, which is highest for stars on heavy favourites, so national scoring leaders tilt toward strong players on average or weak teams.

season_stat_leader.label: CBB season per-game stat leader
season_stat_leader.mechanism: The winner is the maximum over qualified players of a season-long per-game average accumulated over every official game, postseason included. Each average is minutes times a role-driven per-minute rate with large game-to-game noise, thinned by missed games and gated by NCAA minimum qualification, so the probability depends on talent, role stability, availability, how locked the average already is, and which official table settles it.
season_stat_leader.target: Player with the highest season per-game stat (points, threes, etc.) nationally or within a conference, NCAA minimums apply

inputs.why: Per-game 50+ point probability per candidate, a far-tail quantity.
Per-game probability of 10+ in three of five eligible stats per candidate.
Expected games played per candidate from field entry, survival and availability.
Combines correlated player-games into the any-player probability.
Field and survival simulation that drives exposure and is shared across players.
Field size and play-in games set the total number of team-games.
Usage and per-minute rates are the scale of each player's tails.
Joint covariance of counts decides triple-double probability.
Tournament minutes ceiling for stars multiplies every tail.
A candidate's absence removes his whole contribution.
Tournament opponents are stronger and concede fewer counts by role.
Rebound and assist recording errors matter for 10-count thresholds.
First Four included and the five eligible triple-double categories are set here.
Closing-line-independent competitive-versus-blowout regime mixture of the final margin sets the blowout truncation of star minutes.
Fundamentals-only P(regulation tie) and OT-period chain give the chance of extra minutes for stars in a given matchup.
Coach-specific starter-pull behaviour when ahead converts the blowout regime into actual star minutes.
Matchup possessions scale every count; a fast opponent raises both 50-point and triple-double reach.
Field-level frequency of 50-point games and triple-doubles per tournament by era anchors and bounds the bottom-up union.
A teammate's absence concentrates usage, rebounds and assists on the candidate and lifts his tail probabilities.

interactions.hypothesis: A high-tail scorer on a weak team contributes little because he plays one or two games; exposure and tail multiply.
Star minutes rise in close tournament games and fall in first-round blowouts, so the minutes ceiling depends on matchup closeness.
Triple-double probability is driven by joint, not marginal, counts; independence badly misprices it.
Matchup possessions scale attempt volume, so a fast game raises the 50-point reach more than proportionally.

Each player's contribution to the union is roughly per-game tail probability times expected games; a volume scorer on a likely first-round loser adds little, while a moderate-tail star on a 1 seed adds more through five or six games.

In close tournament games stars play near 40 minutes; in blowouts they sit early. The regime is set by the matchup's expected margin, so the minutes ceiling and tail probability switch between two levels rather than shifting smoothly.

Three counts reaching 10 together depend on shared minutes and pace and on role-specific residual correlation; the minutes draw links all categories, so a high-minutes regime raises triple-double probability more than proportionally.

Teammates and opponents share survival paths: if a candidate's team loses early, his games and his teammates' games vanish together, so the union has less effective diversification than independent player-games imply.
Overtime adds about 12 percent more minutes to a full-minute star; because the 50-point event is far in the tail, a modest minutes increase raises its probability by much more than 12 percent.

Possessions scale attempt volume, and the 50-point event sits far in the tail, so a fast matchup raises its probability by more than the possession ratio; a slow game controlled by the opponent pushes the same star far below the 50-point reach.

tournament_player_milestone.label: Any-player tournament milestone (triple-double, 50-point game)
tournament_player_milestone.mechanism: The event is a union over every player-game of the tournament (First Four included). Each player-game's chance is a far-tail probability of his stat distribution given minutes, usage, opponent and game script; exposure is the number of games his team survives. A few high-usage scorers or versatile rebound-and-assist players hold most of the mass, so the outcome depends on which teams make the field, how far they advance, star availability, blowout truncation, overtime and the stat source.
tournament_player_milestone.target: Whether any player in the whole NCAA men's tournament reaches a single-game stat milestone (triple-double, 50+ points)
